claim: Reduced cardiac contractility during heart failure (HF) is linked to impaired Ca2+ release from Ryanodine Receptors (RyRs).
source: Reduced cardiac contractility during heart failure (HF) is linked to impaired Ca2+ release from Ryanodine Receptors (RyRs).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established relationship in the field.

claim: Super-resolution imaging revealed dispersion of RyR clusters in cardiomyocytes from post-infarction HF rats.
source: Using super-resolution imaging, we observed dispersion of RyR clusters in cardiomyocytes from post-infarction HF rats, resulting in more numerous, smaller clusters.
evidence: This is a primary finding from dSTORM imaging experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: RyR cluster dispersion in HF results in more numerous, smaller clusters.
source: Using super-resolution imaging, we observed dispersion of RyR clusters in cardiomyocytes from post-infarction HF rats, resulting in more numerous, smaller clusters.
evidence: This is directly measured and quantified in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: Functional groupings of RyR clusters which produce Ca2+ sparks (Ca2+ release units, CRUs) became less solid in HF.
source: Functional groupings of RyR clusters which produce Ca2+ sparks (Ca2+ release units, CRUs) also became less solid.
evidence: This is measured by convex hull analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: An increased fraction of small CRUs in HF was linked to augmented 'silent' Ca2+ leak, not visible as sparks.
source: An increased fraction of small CRUs in HF was linked to augmented 'silent' Ca2+ leak, not visible as sparks.
evidence: This is supported by microsomal leak measurements (Figure 3) and mathematical modeling (Figure 4).

claim: Larger multi-cluster CRUs common in HF exhibited low fidelity spark generation.
source: Larger multi-cluster CRUs common in HF also exhibited low fidelity spark generation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical modeling in Figure 4B.

claim: Sparks in failing cells displayed slow kinetics as Ca2+ spread across dispersed CRUs.
source: When successfully triggered, sparks in failing cells displayed slow kinetics as Ca2+ spread across dispersed CRUs.
evidence: This is measured experimentally in Figure 5 and reproduced in modeling in Figure 6.

claim: Slow sparks protracted and desynchronized the overall Ca2+ transient during the action potential.
source: During the action potential, these slow sparks protracted and desynchronized the overall Ca2+ transient.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7 showing correlation between slow sparks and local transient kinetics.

claim: Nanoscale RyR reorganization during HF augments Ca2+ leak and slows Ca2+ release kinetics, leading to weakened contraction.
source: Thus, nanoscale RyR reorganization during HF augments Ca2+ leak and slows Ca2+ release kinetics, leading to weakened contraction in this disease.
evidence: This is the main conclusion synthesizing all experimental and modeling results.

claim: Depolarization of the sarcolemma triggers the opening of voltage-gated L-Type Ca2+ channels (LTCCs).
source: Depolarization of the sarcolemma triggers the opening of voltage-gated L-Type Ca2+ channels (LTCCs), and the resulting Ca2+ influx elicits additional Ca2+ release via Ryanodine Receptors (RyRs) in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cardiac excitation-contraction coupling.

claim: Ca2+ influx through LTCCs elicits additional Ca2+ release via RyRs in the SR.
source: Depolarization of the sarcolemma triggers the opening of voltage-gated L-Type Ca2+ channels (LTCCs), and the resulting Ca2+ influx elicits additional Ca2+ release via Ryanodine Receptors (RyRs) in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR).
evidence: This describes the process of Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release, which is established knowledge.

claim: Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release leads to a sharp increase in cytosolic Ca2+ concentration which initiates cardiomyocyte contraction.
source: This process of Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release leads to a sharp increase in cytosolic Ca2+ concentration which initiates cardiomyocyte contraction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about excitation-contraction coupling.

claim: In ventricular myocytes, Ca2+ release is tightly controlled by the arrangement of LTCCs and RyRs in dyads.
source: In ventricular myocytes, Ca2+ release is tightly controlled by the arrangement of LTCCs and RyRs in dyads, with LTCCs present in t-tubules juxtaposed from RyRs across a narrow 12–15 nm dyadic cleft (Bers, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bers, 2001.

claim: LTCCs are present in t-tubules juxtaposed from RyRs across a narrow 12–15 nm dyadic cleft.
source: In ventricular myocytes, Ca2+ release is tightly controlled by the arrangement of LTCCs and RyRs in dyads, with LTCCs present in t-tubules juxtaposed from RyRs across a narrow 12–15 nm dyadic cleft (Bers, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bers, 2001.

claim: RyRs are organized into clusters.
source: The RyRs themselves are organized into clusters; an arrangement that couples their gating, promoting synchronized opening and closing of neighbouring channels (Marx et al., 2001; Sobie et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marx et al., 2001 and Sobie et al., 2006.

claim: RyR clustering couples their gating, promoting synchronized opening and closing of neighbouring channels.
source: The RyRs themselves are organized into clusters; an arrangement that couples their gating, promoting synchronized opening and closing of neighbouring channels (Marx et al., 2001; Sobie et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marx et al., 2001 and Sobie et al., 2006.

claim: Neighbouring clusters of RyRs can act concertedly if the Ca2+ diffusion distance between them is sufficiently short.
source: Recent data have indicated that neighbouring clusters of RyRs can also act concertedly if the Ca2+ diffusion distance between them is sufficiently short (Macquaide et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Macquaide et al., 2015.

claim: Functional arrangements of RyR clusters are referred to as 'superclusters' or Ca2+ Release Units (CRUs).
source: Referred to as 'superclusters' or Ca2+ Release Units (CRUs), these functional arrangements of RyR clusters generate Ca2+ sparks, the fundamental units of SR Ca2+ release in cardiomyocytes (Cheng et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cheng et al., 1993.

claim: CRUs generate Ca2+ sparks, the fundamental units of SR Ca2+ release in cardiomyocytes.
source: Referred to as 'superclusters' or Ca2+ Release Units (CRUs), these functional arrangements of RyR clusters generate Ca2+ sparks, the fundamental units of SR Ca2+ release in cardiomyocytes (Cheng et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cheng et al., 1993.

claim: Ca2+ sparks are elicited by LTCC opening.
source: Ca2+ sparks are not only elicited by LTCC opening, but also occur spontaneously during diastole, where spark frequency and geometry can be measured to assess CRU function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ca2+ spark generation.

claim: Ca2+ sparks occur spontaneously during diastole.
source: Ca2+ sparks are not only elicited by LTCC opening, but also occur spontaneously during diastole, where spark frequency and geometry can be measured to assess CRU function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ca2+ spark generation.

claim: Spark frequency and geometry can be measured to assess CRU function.
source: Ca2+ sparks are not only elicited by LTCC opening, but also occur spontaneously during diastole, where spark frequency and geometry can be measured to assess CRU function.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about how CRU function is assessed.

claim: Ca2+ sparks are an important source of RyR-mediated Ca2+ leak from the SR.
source: While Ca2+ sparks are an important source of RyR-mediated Ca2+ leak from the SR, 'silent' or 'non-spark' events also occur, and involve the opening of a subset of RyRs within a CRU; so-called 'quarky' release (Brochet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Brochet et al., 2011.

claim: 'Silent' or 'non-spark' Ca2+ release events occur and involve the opening of a subset of RyRs within a CRU.
source: While Ca2+ sparks are an important source of RyR-mediated Ca2+ leak from the SR, 'silent' or 'non-spark' events also occur, and involve the opening of a subset of RyRs within a CRU; so-called 'quarky' release (Brochet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brochet et al., 2011.

claim: Silent Ca2+ release is referred to as 'quarky' release.
source: While Ca2+ sparks are an important source of RyR-mediated Ca2+ leak from the SR, 'silent' or 'non-spark' events also occur, and involve the opening of a subset of RyRs within a CRU; so-called 'quarky' release (Brochet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brochet et al., 2011.

claim: Impaired cardiomyocyte Ca2+ homeostasis contributes to reduced cardiac contractility and arrhythmogenesis in heart failure.
source: Impaired cardiomyocyte Ca2+ homeostasis is believed to importantly contribute to reduced cardiac contractility and arrhythmogenesis in heart failure (HF).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of heart failure research.

claim: SR Ca2+ release is reduced and slowed in heart failure.
source: SR Ca2+ release is reduced and slowed in this condition, and these changes have been linked to altered dyadic structure (Louch et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Louch et al., 2010.

claim: Reduced and slowed SR Ca2+ release in HF has been linked to altered dyadic structure.
source: SR Ca2+ release is reduced and slowed in this condition, and these changes have been linked to altered dyadic structure (Louch et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Louch et al., 2010.

claim: Marked remodeling of the t-tubular system occurs in failing cardiomyocytes.
source: We and others have observed marked remodeling of the t-tubular system in failing cardiomyocytes, while RyRs remain predominantly distributed along z-lines (Song et al., 2006; Louch et al., 2006; Heinzel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Song et al., 2006; Louch et al., 2006; Heinzel et al., 2008.

claim: RyRs remain predominantly distributed along z-lines in failing cardiomyocytes.
source: We and others have observed marked remodeling of the t-tubular system in failing cardiomyocytes, while RyRs remain predominantly distributed along z-lines (Song et al., 2006; Louch et al., 2006; Heinzel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Song et al., 2006; Louch et al., 2006; Heinzel et al., 2008.

claim: Coupling between LTCCs and RyRs is disrupted in heart failure.
source: Thus, the coupling between LTCCs and RyRs is disrupted, with 'orphaned' CRUs exhibiting delayed Ca2+ release only after trigger Ca2+ diffuses from intact dyads.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of t-tubule remodeling while RyRs remain at z-lines.

claim: 'Orphaned' CRUs exhibit delayed Ca2+ release only after trigger Ca2+ diffuses from intact dyads.
source: Thus, the coupling between LTCCs and RyRs is disrupted, with 'orphaned' CRUs exhibiting delayed Ca2+ release only after trigger Ca2+ diffuses from intact dyads.
evidence: This is inferred from the disruption of LTCC-RyR coupling.

claim: Abnormal gaps between t-tubules only account for a fraction of the overall de-synchronization of Ca2+ release in HF.
source: However, abnormal gaps occurring between t-tubules only account for a fraction of the overall de-synchronization of Ca2+ release in HF (Louch et al., 2006; Øyehaug et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Louch et al., 2006; Øyehaug et al., 2013.

claim: Other alterations at the nanometer scale of CRU organization might hinder efficient triggering of Ca2+ release in HF.
source: This suggests that other alterations might also occur, perhaps at the nanometer scale of CRU organization, which hinder efficient triggering of Ca2+ release.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that t-tubule gaps don't fully explain Ca2+ release desynchronization.

claim: CRU reorganization could contribute to increased Ca2+ leak, including silent leak, which is a hallmark of heart failure.
source: CRU reorganization could in principle contribute to increased Ca2+ leak, including silent leak, which is a hallmark of heart failure (Zima et al., 2010; Walker et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculated and supported by citations to Zima et al., 2010; Walker et al., 2014.

claim: Exaggerated Ca2+ leak in failing cells has been linked to reduced SR Ca2+ content and depressed contractile function.
source: Exaggerated Ca2+ leak in failing cells has been linked to reduced SR Ca2+ content and depressed contractile function, elevation of resting Ca2+ levels and impaired relaxation, pro-arrhythmic early and delayed afterdepolarizations, and energetic inefficiency as Ca2+ is redundantly cycled (Bers, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bers, 2014.

claim: Exaggerated Ca2+ leak in failing cells has been linked to elevation of resting Ca2+ levels and impaired relaxation.
source: Exaggerated Ca2+ leak in failing cells has been linked to reduced SR Ca2+ content and depressed contractile function, elevation of resting Ca2+ levels and impaired relaxation, pro-arrhythmic early and delayed afterdepolarizations, and energetic inefficiency as Ca2+ is redundantly cycled (Bers, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bers, 2014.

claim: Exaggerated Ca2+ leak in failing cells has been linked to pro-arrhythmic early and delayed afterdepolarizations.
source: Exaggerated Ca2+ leak in failing cells has been linked to reduced SR Ca2+ content and depressed contractile function, elevation of resting Ca2+ levels and impaired relaxation, pro-arrhythmic early and delayed afterdepolarizations, and energetic inefficiency as Ca2+ is redundantly cycled (Bers, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bers, 2014.

claim: Exaggerated Ca2+ leak in failing cells has been linked to energetic inefficiency as Ca2+ is redundantly cycled.
source: Exaggerated Ca2+ leak in failing cells has been linked to reduced SR Ca2+ content and depressed contractile function, elevation of resting Ca2+ levels and impaired relaxation, pro-arrhythmic early and delayed afterdepolarizations, and energetic inefficiency as Ca2+ is redundantly cycled (Bers, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bers, 2014.

claim: Super-resolution microscopy techniques have markedly improved the ability to visualize and quantify CRU organization.
source: The advent of super-resolution microscopy techniques has markedly improved our ability to visualize and quantify CRU organization (Baddeley et al., 2009; Macquaide et al., 2015; Jayasinghe et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baddeley et al., 2009; Macquaide et al., 2015; Jayasinghe et al., 2018.

claim: Super-resolution techniques have not previously been employed to examine RyR configuration in HF.
source: However, these techniques have not previously been employed to examine RyR configuration in HF.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study.

claim: Using confocal imaging and SIM, the localization of RyRs along z-Lines was clearly apparent, but organization of RyRs within CRUs was not discernable.
source: Using diffraction-limited confocal imaging (resolution ≈250 nm) and Structured Illumination Microscopy (SIM, resolution ≈120 nm), the localization of RyRs along z-Lines was clearly apparent, but organization of RyRs within CRUs was not discernable (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1A comparing different imaging modalities.

claim: dSTORM imaging provided mean localization precision of 21 ± 3 nm.
source: With dSTORM imaging, spatial resolution was markedly improved (mean localization precision = 21 ± 3 nm) enabling detailed CRU geometry to be assessed.
evidence: This is a measurement of the technical performance of the dSTORM imaging.

claim: Overall RyR expression was similar in Sham and HF, as evidenced by Western blotting of ventricular homogenates.
source: Overall RyR expression was similar in Sham and HF, as evidenced by Western blotting of ventricular homogenates (Figure 2— figure supplement 1), and equivalent RyR labeling density in cardiomyocytes (41.9 ± 1.4 RyR/µm, 40.4 ± 1.3 RyR/µm in Sham, HF respectively).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: RyR labeling density was equivalent in Sham and HF cardiomyocytes (41.9 ± 1.4 RyR/µm in Sham, 40.4 ± 1.3 RyR/µm in HF).
source: Overall RyR expression was similar in Sham and HF, as evidenced by Western blotting of ventricular homogenates (Figure 2— figure supplement 1), and equivalent RyR labeling density in cardiomyocytes (41.9 ± 1.4 RyR/µm, 40.4 ± 1.3 RyR/µm in Sham, HF respectively).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from dSTORM imaging.

claim: In both Sham and HF groups, RyR staining showed a predominantly transverse, striated pattern.
source: In both groups, RyR staining showed a predominantly transverse, striated pattern (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Nanoscale dSTORM imaging revealed fragmentation of RyR clusters in failing cardiomyocytes.
source: However, despite rather similar organization of RyRs at the macroscale, nanoscale dSTORM imaging revealed fragmentation of RyR clusters in failing cardiomyocytes (see insets in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the insets of Figure 2A.

claim: Cluster breakup resulted in a reduction in the number of RyRs per cluster in HF.
source: Cluster breakup resulted in a reduction in the number of RyRs per cluster, and a greater proportion of small clusters in HF (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 2B.

claim: HF resulted in a greater proportion of small RyR clusters.
source: Cluster breakup resulted in a reduction in the number of RyRs per cluster, and a greater proportion of small clusters in HF (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 2B.

claim: The overall number of RyR clusters increased in failing cells.
source: The overall number of clusters increased accordingly in failing cells (Figure 2D), and inter-cluster distance was reduced (Figure 2E; see Figure 2—source data 1 for mean data across animals).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 2D.

claim: Inter-cluster distance was reduced in HF.
source: The overall number of clusters increased accordingly in failing cells (Figure 2D), and inter-cluster distance was reduced (Figure 2E; see Figure 2—source data 1 for mean data across animals).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 2E.

claim: The number of clusters contained in a CRU increased in HF.
source: Consistent with fragmentation of clusters into smaller adjacent groupings, the number of clusters contained in a CRU increased in HF (Figure 2F), although the number of RyRs per CRU decreased (Figure 2C) since RyR clusters were markedly reduced in size.
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 2F.

claim: The number of RyRs per CRU decreased in HF.
source: Consistent with fragmentation of clusters into smaller adjacent groupings, the number of clusters contained in a CRU increased in HF (Figure 2F), although the number of RyRs per CRU decreased (Figure 2C) since RyR clusters were markedly reduced in size.
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 2C.

claim: CRU solidity decreased in HF.
source: Convex hull analysis (see methods) revealed a consequent decrease in CRU solidity in HF (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 2G using convex hull analysis.

claim: RyR reorganization in failing cells resulted in CRUs with a more sparse, dispersed configuration of smaller sub-clusters.
source: Thus, RyR reorganization in failing cells resulted in CRUs with a more sparse, dispersed configuration of smaller sub-clusters.
evidence: This is a summary of the structural findings from Figure 2.

claim: The Ca2+ leak rate was markedly higher in HF compared to Sham in SR microsomes.
source: The Ca2+ leak rate was markedly higher in HF compared to Sham (inset in Figure 3A, mean data in Figure 3C).
evidence: This is measured in microsomal preparations and shown in Figure 3A and 3C.

claim: SR Ca2+ uptake was significantly slowed in HF.
source: In agreement with previous work (reviewed in Bers, 2006), we additionally observed significantly slowed SR Ca2+ uptake in HF (Figure 3B) and lower Ca2+ content (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is measured in microsomal preparations and shown in Figure 3B, with citation to Bers, 2006.

claim: SR Ca2+ content was lower in HF.
source: In agreement with previous work (reviewed in Bers, 2006), we additionally observed significantly slowed SR Ca2+ uptake in HF (Figure 3B) and lower Ca2+ content (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is measured in microsomal preparations and shown in Figure 3D, with citation to Bers, 2006.

claim: Ca2+ spark mass was significantly increased in HF cells.
source: While the average Ca2+ release per spark (spark mass) was significantly increased in HF cells, this effect was offset by a tendency toward lower spark frequency (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is measured by confocal linescan imaging and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Spark frequency tended to be lower in HF cells.
source: While the average Ca2+ release per spark (spark mass) was significantly increased in HF cells, this effect was offset by a tendency toward lower spark frequency (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is measured by confocal linescan imaging and shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Overall spark-mediated Ca2+ leak was similar in HF and Sham cells.
source: Indeed, overall spark-mediated Ca2+ leak was similar in HF and Sham cells (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is calculated from spark measurements and shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The observation of increased total RyR leak but similar spark-mediated leak is consistent with augmented 'silent', non-spark mediated leak in failing cells.
source: Since we observed an increase in total RyR leak in HF, these results are consistent with augmented 'silent', non-spark mediated leak in failing cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between total leak and spark-mediated leak measurements.

claim: Ca2+ release from the smallest idealized CRUs (4 RyRs) was never detected as sparks in simulations.
source: Ca2+ release from the smallest CRUs was never detected, but a progressively greater proportion of events yielded visible sparks as the number of RyRs in these idealized dyad geometries was increased (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown by mathematical modeling in Figure 4A.

claim: A progressively greater proportion of simulated Ca2+ release events yielded visible sparks as the number of RyRs in idealized CRUs was increased.
source: Ca2+ release from the smallest CRUs was never detected, but a progressively greater proportion of events yielded visible sparks as the number of RyRs in these idealized dyad geometries was increased (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown by mathematical modeling in Figure 4A.

claim: Single-cluster CRUs exhibited high Ca2+ spark fidelity in simulations.
source: While the single-cluster CRU exhibited high Ca2+ spark fidelity, lower probability of spark generation was observed in dispersed, multi-cluster CRUs (fidelity indicated by colour scale).
evidence: This is shown by mathematical modeling in Figure 4B.

claim: Lower probability of spark generation was observed in dispersed, multi-cluster CRUs in simulations.
source: While the single-cluster CRU exhibited high Ca2+ spark fidelity, lower probability of spark generation was observed in dispersed, multi-cluster CRUs (fidelity indicated by colour scale).
evidence: This is shown by mathematical modeling in Figure 4B.

claim: CRU rearrangement during HF promotes silent RyR leak due to an increased fraction of small CRUs.
source: These data support that CRU rearrangement during HF promotes silent RyR leak, due to an increased fraction of both small CRUs as well as larger CRUs with dispersed, irregular configurations.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling results in Figure 4.

claim: CRU rearrangement during HF promotes silent RyR leak due to larger CRUs with dispersed, irregular configurations.
source: These data support that CRU rearrangement during HF promotes silent RyR leak, due to an increased fraction of both small CRUs as well as larger CRUs with dispersed, irregular configurations.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling results in Figure 4.

claim: Spark kinetics in Sham cells generally exhibited rapid rising and declining phases.
source: Spark kinetics in Sham cells generally exhibited rapid rising and declining phases.
evidence: This is observed in the representative data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Some sparks in HF cells exhibited markedly slow rise and decay kinetics.
source: While some sparks also showed fast kinetics in HF cells, others were markedly slow to rise and decay (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is observed in the representative data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Spark rise time and duration exhibited broader distributions in HF compared to Sham.
source: Indeed, measurements of spark rise time and duration exhibited broader distributions and were, on the average, prolonged in HF compared to Sham (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5B.

claim: Mean spark rise time and duration were prolonged in HF compared to Sham.
source: Indeed, measurements of spark rise time and duration exhibited broader distributions and were, on the average, prolonged in HF compared to Sham (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5B.

claim: RyR opening times were delayed in dispersed, multi-cluster CRUs compared to solid, single-cluster CRUs in simulations.
source: Representative simulations show that RyR opening times were delayed in the dispersed, multi-cluster CRUs compared to the solid, single-cluster CRU (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown by mathematical modeling in Figure 6A.

claim: Delayed RyR openings in multi-cluster CRUs resulted in more variable kinetics and overall slowing of spark rise time in simulations.
source: Simulations of Ca2+ spark time courses further showed that the delayed RyR openings in multi-cluster CRUs resulted in more variable kinetics and overall slowing of spark rise time (Figure 6B, mean data Figure 6C), reproducing experimental observations.
evidence: This is shown by mathematical modeling in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Simply reducing the RyR number in the mathematical model did not markedly alter Ca2+ spark kinetics.
source: Of note, although CRUs were observed to contain fewer RyRs in HF than Sham (Figure 2C), simply reducing the RyR number to an equivalent degree in the mathematical model did not markedly alter Ca2+ spark kinetics (Figure 6—source data 1), further confirming a key role of CRU fragmentation in failing cells.
evidence: This is shown by additional modeling results in Figure 6—source data 1.

claim: Field-stimulated Ca2+ transients were significantly slower to rise in HF than Sham.
source: We observed that field-stimulated Ca2+ transients were significantly slower to rise in HF than Sham (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is measured by confocal linescan imaging and shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: Slowing of Ca2+ release in HF was associated with marked de-synchronization of the Ca2+ transient.
source: This slowing of Ca2+ release was associated with marked de-synchronization of the Ca2+ transient, which we quantified by measuring the variability in time to reach half-maximal fluorescence (TTF50) across the cell (see lower panels in Figure 7A).
evidence: This is measured by confocal linescan imaging and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The dyssynchrony index was significantly increased in HF compared to Sham, with a strongly right-shifted distribution of values.
source: This 'dyssynchrony index' (Louch et al., 2006) was significantly increased in HF compared to Sham, with a strongly right-shifted distribution of values (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 7D, with citation to Louch et al., 2006.

claim: T-tubule disruption in failing cells has been previously established in the post-infarction HF rat model.
source: T-tubule disruption in failing cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) has been previously established in this model of HF (Frisk et al., 2016), and is a recognized cause of Ca2+ release dyssynchrony in this disease (Song et al., 2006; Louch et al., 2006; Heinzel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and supported by citations to Frisk et al., 2016; Song et al., 2006; Louch et al., 2006; Heinzel et al., 2008.

claim: T-tubule disruption is a recognized cause of Ca2+ release dyssynchrony in heart failure.
source: T-tubule disruption in failing cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) has been previously established in this model of HF (Frisk et al., 2016), and is a recognized cause of Ca2+ release dyssynchrony in this disease (Song et al., 2006; Louch et al., 2006; Heinzel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Song et al., 2006; Louch et al., 2006; Heinzel et al., 2008.

claim: 24% of sparks in HF cells were defined as slow (rise time >13 ms), while only 13% of Sham sparks fit this definition.
source: By this definition, 24% of sparks in HF cells were defined as slow, while only 13% of Sham sparks fit this definition.
evidence: This is calculated from the spark measurements.

claim: Local transients from slow spark locations in HF exhibited markedly slower rise times than those from fast spark locations in both HF and Sham.
source: Local transients from slow spark locations in HF exhibited markedly slower rise times than those from fast spark locations in both HF and Sham (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The association between slow sparks and slow local transients was apparent in 'heat map' plots.
source: The association between slow sparks and slow local transients was also apparent in 'heat map' plots (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7G.

claim: By protracting Ca2+ sparks, CRU dispersion during HF slows and desynchronizes the overall Ca2+ transient.
source: These results show that by protracting Ca2+ sparks, CRU dispersion during HF slows and desynchronizes the overall Ca2+ transient.
evidence: This is concluded from the correlation between slow sparks and slow local transients shown in Figure 7.

claim: An average cluster contains approximately 14 RyRs in healthy, Sham-operated rat ventricular cells.
source: Using images collected close to the cell surface (depth of 200 – 500 nm, see also Macquaide et al. [Macquaide et al., 2015]), we calculated that an average cluster contains approximately 14 RyRs in our healthy, Sham-operated rat ventricular cells.
evidence: This is calculated from dSTORM imaging data.

claim: The estimation of 14 RyRs/cluster is in close agreement with previous estimates made at the cell surface.
source: This estimation is in close agreement with previous estimates made at the cell surface (14 RyRs/cluster) (Baddeley et al., 2009), but considerably lower than estimates made deep within the cell interior (Hou et al., 2015), a discrepancy which may reflect regional differences in RyR organization across the cell.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baddeley et al., 2009.

claim: Average CRUs contain roughly 3-4 clusters and a total of ≈30 RyRs when using a 150 nm CRU definition.
source: Assuming that RyR clusters located within 150 nm cooperatively form a CRU (Macquaide et al., 2015), we calculated that average CRUs contain roughly 3 – 4 clusters, and a total of ≈30 RyRs.
evidence: This is calculated from dSTORM imaging data with citation to Macquaide et al., 2015.

claim: Using a 100 nm CRU definition, average CRU size was reduced to ≈25 RyRs.
source: Using a narrower CRU definition, with inclusion of neighbouring clusters within 100 nm (Baddeley et al., 2009; Hou et al., 2015), reduced average CRU size to ≈25 RyRs (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is calculated from dSTORM imaging data with citations to Baddeley et al., 2009; Hou et al., 2015.

claim: An electron microscopy tomography study reported that an average-sized dyad could hold up to 43 RyRs, with RyRs occupying ≈78% of the dyadic space (≈34 RyRs/CRU).
source: The authors reported that while there was great variability in CRU size and geometry, dyadic volume was an order of magnitude lower than previous estimates (Franzini-Armstrong et al., 1999; Scriven et al., 2013); an average-sized dyad could only hold up to 43 RyRs, with RyRs occupying ≈78% of the dyadic space (≈34 RyRs/CRU).
evidence: This is cited from an electron microscopy tomography study of mouse ventricular cardiomyocytes (Hayashi et al., 2009).

claim: Typical sparks result from the activation of ≈20–30 RyRs.
source: It is estimated that typical sparks result from the activation of somewhat fewer RyRs, ≈20–30 (Shkryl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shkryl et al., 2012.

claim: 42% of CRUs contained five or fewer RyRs in Sham cells.
source: Consistent with previous work (Baddeley et al., 2009; Hayashi et al., 2009; Hou et al., 2015), we observed that many CRUs have very small geometry even in healthy cells; 42% of CRUs contained five or fewer RyRs in Sham (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is calculated from dSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 2C, with citations to Baddeley et al., 2009; Hayashi et al., 2009; Hou et al., 2015.

claim: Silent, non-spark mediated leak is a significant contributor to overall RyR leak.
source: Previous work by Zima et al. has shown that silent, non-spark mediated leak is a significant contributor to overall RyR leak (Zima et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zima et al., 2010.

claim: The decreased fidelity of spark triggering in dispersed CRUs results from the spacing between neighbouring clusters, which inhibits cooperative, diffusion-based triggering.
source: Our results show that the decreased fidelity of spark triggering in these dispersed CRUs results from the spacing between neighbouring clusters, which inhibits cooperative, diffusion-based triggering.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Released Ca2+ more easily escapes from less densely packed CRUs, making it less likely to trigger additional RyRs.
source: Furthermore, released Ca2+ more easily escapes from less densely packed CRUs, making it less likely to trigger additional RyRs.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Spark fidelity declined when clusters deviated from circular and compact shapes.
source: This finding is in agreement with previous modeling studies showing that spark fidelity declined when clusters deviated from circular and compact shapes (Walker et al., 2014), and that RyR activation during triggered release is less likely when CRUs are broken into sub-clusters (Cannell and Soeller, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Walker et al., 2014 and Cannell and Soeller, 1997.

claim: RyR activation during triggered release is less likely when CRUs are broken into sub-clusters.
source: This finding is in agreement with previous modeling studies showing that spark fidelity declined when clusters deviated from circular and compact shapes (Walker et al., 2014), and that RyR activation during triggered release is less likely when CRUs are broken into sub-clusters (Cannell and Soeller, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cannell and Soeller, 1997.

claim: Increased RyR leak during heart failure is widely believed to promote arrhythmia via generation of both early and delayed afterdepolarizations.
source: Increased RyR leak during heart failure is widely believed to promote arrhythmia via generation of both early and delayed afterdepolarizations.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, as indicated by the phrase 'widely believed'.

claim: Greater RyR leak promotes depression of contraction via loss of SR Ca2+ content.
source: Furthermore, greater leak also promotes depression of contraction, via loss of SR Ca2+ content, and poor relaxation, due to elevation of resting Ca2+ (reviewed in Bers, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bers, 2014.

claim: Greater RyR leak promotes poor relaxation due to elevation of resting Ca2+.
source: Furthermore, greater leak also promotes depression of contraction, via loss of SR Ca2+ content, and poor relaxation, due to elevation of resting Ca2+ (reviewed in Bers, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bers, 2014.

claim: Prolonged rise time of the Ca2+ transient during HF has been previously linked to slowed isolated cardiomyocyte contraction in both animals and patients.
source: Prolonged rise time of the Ca2+ transient during HF (Figure 7A–C) has been previously linked to slowed isolated cardiomyocyte contraction in both animals (Bokenes et al., 2008; Mørk et al., 2009) and patients (Davies et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bokenes et al., 2008; Mørk et al., 2009; Davies et al., 1995.

claim: In vivo systolic tissue velocity is reduced in HF patients, which decreases contractile power.
source: In vivo systolic tissue velocity is also reduced in HF patients (Vinereanu et al., 2005) which decreases contractile power.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vinereanu et al., 2005.

claim: Spark kinetics were relatively insensitive to changes in RyR number for medium-sized CRUs.
source: Indeed, we observed that spark kinetics were relatively insensitive to changes in RyR number for medium-sized CRUs, in agreement with previous work (Cannell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is observed in modeling results and supported by citation to Cannell et al., 2013.

claim: RyR clustering allows the channels to be functionally coupled, whereby they exhibit coordinated opening and closing.
source: Previous work has shown that RyR clustering allows the channels to be functionally coupled, whereby they exhibit coordinated opening and closing (Marx et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2004; Sobie et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marx et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2004; Sobie et al., 2006.

claim: Thermodynamic stability is lost when RyRs are present alone or with a small number of neighbouring channels, and slow Ca2+ release kinetics result.
source: Wang and colleagues reported that this thermodynamic stability is lost when RyRs are present alone or with a small number of neighbouring channels, and slow Ca2+ release kinetics result (Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2004.

claim: Sparks occurred almost exclusively at t-tubule sites in both healthy and failing cells.
source: In previous work, we (Louch et al., 2013) and others (Meethal et al., 2007) employed simultaneous imaging of t-tubules and Ca2+ and observed that sparks occurred almost exclusively at t-tubule sites in both healthy and failing cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Louch et al., 2013 and Meethal et al., 2007.

claim: De-tubulation experiments dramatically reduced the occurrence of Ca2+ sparks in the cell interior, suggesting that SR-t-tubule junctions are important for spark initiation.
source: Similarly, de-tubulation experiments have been shown to dramatically reduce the occurrence of Ca2+ sparks in the cell interior, suggesting that SR-t-tubule junctions are important for spark initiation (Brette et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brette et al., 2005.

claim: RyRs are not firmly anchored within the CRU, but exhibit a highly malleable organization dependent on factors such as phosphorylation status and cytosolic Mg2+ levels.
source: Emerging data indicate that RyRs are not firmly anchored within the CRU, but exhibit a highly malleable organization dependent on factors such as phosphorylation status and cytosolic Mg2+ levels (Asghari et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Asghari et al., 2014.

claim: Junctophilin-2 (JPH-2) anchors the t-tubule to the SR.
source: Another important dyadic regulator is Junctophilin-2 (JPH-2), which anchors the t-tubule to the SR (Takeshima et al., 2000; Minamisawa et al., 2004), and interacts with the RyR (Beavers et al., 2013; Munro et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Takeshima et al., 2000; Minamisawa et al., 2004.

claim: JPH-2 interacts with the RyR.
source: Another important dyadic regulator is Junctophilin-2 (JPH-2), which anchors the t-tubule to the SR (Takeshima et al., 2000; Minamisawa et al., 2004), and interacts with the RyR (Beavers et al., 2013; Munro et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beavers et al., 2013; Munro et al., 2016.

claim: JPH-2 levels regulate RyR clustering; JPH-2 overexpression triggered the formation of larger RyR clusters.
source: Munro et al recently reported that JPH-2 levels regulate RyR clustering; however, while they observed that JPH-2 overexpression triggered the formation of larger RyR clusters, JPH-2 knockdown did not reduce cluster size (Munro et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Munro et al., 2016.

claim: JPH-2 knockdown did not reduce RyR cluster size.
source: Munro et al recently reported that JPH-2 levels regulate RyR clustering; however, while they observed that JPH-2 overexpression triggered the formation of larger RyR clusters, JPH-2 knockdown did not reduce cluster size (Munro et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Munro et al., 2016.

claim: JPH-2 protein levels were not reduced in the rat HF model used in this study.
source: Although others have observed JPH-2 loss during HF (Minamisawa et al., 2004; Wei et al., 2010), we did not presently observe reduced JP-2 protein levels in our rat HF model (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that JP-2 downregulation is not a prerequisite for reorganization of CRUs (Figure 2) or t-tubules (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, with citations to Minamisawa et al., 2004; Wei et al., 2010.

claim: BIN1 is a well-established regulator of t-tubule growth and structure.
source: Another dyadic regulator, BIN1, is a well-established regulator of t-tubule growth and structure (Hong et al., 2014), and recent data have suggested that this protein may also attract phosphorylated RyRs to the dyad (Fu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hong et al., 2014.

claim: BIN1 may attract phosphorylated RyRs to the dyad.
source: Another dyadic regulator, BIN1, is a well-established regulator of t-tubule growth and structure (Hong et al., 2014), and recent data have suggested that this protein may also attract phosphorylated RyRs to the dyad (Fu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fu et al., 2016.

claim: BIN1 expression is unaltered in the rat HF model used in this study.
source: Although BIN1 loss has been reported in other HF models (Lyon et al., 2012; Caldwell et al., 2014), our data indicate that BIN1 expression is unaltered in our rat model (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, with citations to Lyon et al., 2012; Caldwell et al., 2014.

claim: T-tubule structure is impressively malleable and degraded during heart failure.
source: While previous work has shown that t-tubule structure is impressively malleable, and degraded during heart failure, our present findings show that there is also detrimental reorganization of RyRs in this disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Large anterolateral myocardial infarctions were induced in ~300 g male Wistar-Hannover rats by ligation of the left coronary artery.
source: Large anterolateral myocardial infarctions were induced in ~300 g male Wistar-Hannover rats, by ligation of the left coronary artery as previously described (Lunde et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the experimental method for creating the HF model, with citation to Lunde et al., 2012.

claim: Development of HF was verified six weeks after infarction using echocardiography.
source: Development of HF was verified six weeks later using a Vevo 2100 echocardiography imaging system (VisualSonics, Toronto, Canada).
evidence: This describes the experimental method for verifying HF.

claim: Inclusion of failing animals was based on established criteria including dilation of the left atrium (diameter >5 mm) and ventricle, and increased lung weight (>2.5 g).
source: Inclusion of failing animals was based on established criteria (Sjaastad et al., 2000), including dilation of the left atrium (diameter >5 mm) and ventricle, and increased lung weight (>2.5 g).
evidence: This describes the experimental criteria for HF inclusion, with citation to Sjaastad et al., 2000.

claim: Marked remodeling of t-tubular structure was observed in HF in the post-infarction rat model.
source: In agreement with previous work employing the same post-infarction rat model (Frisk et al., 2016), we observed marked remodeling of t-tubular structure in HF.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1, with citation to Frisk et al., 2016.

claim: T-tubule reorganization in HF included a loss of transverse t-tubule elements and the appearance of additional longitudinal tubules.
source: Skeletonized images (C, D) indicate that this reorganization included a loss of transverse t-tubule elements (colored white) and the appearance of additional longitudinal tubules running in the axial, perpendicular orientation (colored red).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D.
